claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoscale platinum-group metal catalyst has a native, largely reduced surface.
A mild oxidation pretreatment or slightly oxidizing electrolyte will generate a moderate surface oxide layer on the catalyst.
A potential window exists in acidic electrolyte in which the surface oxide is stable and active without being overoxidized.
Oxide formation and stability at defect or edge sites govern catalyst behavior.
Transient surface oxide creates active sites that stabilize key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Stabilization of key intermediates by the surface oxide lowers the activation energy for complete ethanol oxidation.
The surface oxide changes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its intermediates.
Oxide-induced changes in adsorption energies promote proton-coupled electron transfer during ethanol oxidation.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves twelve-electron and twelve-proton transfer.
The surface oxide facilitates conversion of poisoning intermediates to carbon dioxide.
Facilitating conversion of poisoning intermediates reduces their accumulation on the catalyst.
The surface oxide may suppress nanoparticle agglomeration during operation.
The surface oxide may suppress dissolution of platinum-group metal atoms during operation.
Suppression of poisoning, agglomeration, or dissolution enhances catalyst durability.
An optimally oxidized catalyst will exhibit higher current density than the untreated catalyst.
An optimally oxidized catalyst will exhibit greater selectivity for complete oxidation to carbon dioxide than the untreated catalyst.
An optimally oxidized catalyst will retain performance for longer than the untreated catalyst.
The proposed benefit will occur only under moderate oxidation conditions.
At low potentials, insufficient oxide formation will cause the proposed improvements to diminish or disappear.
At excessively high potentials, oxide reduction or overoxidation will cause the proposed improvements to diminish or disappear.

contradictions.description: The oxide is described as transient in the hypothesis but as moderate, stable, or stability-governing elsewhere; the intended oxide lifetime during operation is therefore ambiguous.
The conditions associate excessively high potential with overoxidation, whereas the boundary also suggests that the oxide may be absent at excessively high potential because of reduction.
